name: Salalah International Airport
before:
Oman's second international airport after Muscat, on the coastal plain 5.5 km north east of Salalah in the Dhofar Governorate.

The season is the thing to understand here. Salalah is at its busiest from July to September, when the Asian monsoon reaches this stretch of coast and brings the Khareef, turning green a part of the Gulf that is arid the rest of the year. Other Gulf carriers long flew here only during the Khareef, and Air India was the first to run international services year round, opening Kozhikode and then Cochin.

The terminal is newer than the airport's history suggests, with four air conditioned airbridges, a duty free area and an Oman Air lounge opposite the gates for Business and First passengers and for Gold and Silver Sinbad cardholders.

It began in 1935 as a Royal Air Force airfield and stayed military through the Jebel Akhdar and Dhofar wars, opening to civilian traffic in 1977. The Royal Air Force of Oman still shares the site.
after:
Salalah's airport, in the Dhofar Governorate, north of the city centre. Its present terminal opened in 2015.

The season is the thing to understand here. Tourism peaks in the Khareef, the summer monsoon season, when light rain falls on Dhofar.

Oman Air and SalamAir both fly to Muscat, and Air India Express to Kozhikode (Calicut) in India. There is an Oman Air lounge for first and business class passengers and Sindbad members, and a duty free area.

It began as an RAF airfield, and the RAF left in 1977.

The FCDO reports Iranian strikes and retaliatory attacks in Oman and elsewhere in the region since 8 July 2026 and tells British nationals in the Middle East to be prepared for flight cancellations and periodic airspace closures.

claims.claim: began as an RAF airfield; the RAF left in 1977
claims.inAfter: It began as an RAF airfield, and the RAF left in 1977.
claims.note: Was 'began in 1935 as a Royal Air Force airfield'. Wikipedia gives 1935, but rafweb.org (Air of Authority, a history of RAF organisation) lists RAF squadron detachments at Salalah from February 1927, so the start date is dropped. Both agree the RAF station closed in 1977 (rafweb: 31 March 1977). Historical, not time-sensitive. Reworded in review (23 Sep): the RAF station closed in 1977, not the airfield, which rafweb notes is now Salalah Airport.

claims.claim: Oman's second international airport after Muscat
claims.wasBefore: Oman's second international airport after Muscat, on the coastal plain 5.5 km north east of Salalah in the Dhofar Governorate.
claims.why: The rank is time-sensitive and only Wikipedia and rafweb.org (undated) give it. The CAA's 'Yearly statistics 2025' file is a lorem-ipsum placeholder and its monthly figures are spreadsheets the fetchers cannot save as text. The distance fails the coordinates check and the sources disagree on it (see the direction claim). 'Coastal plain' has only Wikipedia; the operator calls it the Ittin plain.

claims.claim: busiest July to September; Khareef turns the arid Gulf green
claims.wasBefore: Salalah is at its busiest from July to September, when the Asian monsoon reaches this stretch of coast and brings the Khareef, turning green a part of the Gulf that is arid the rest of the year.
claims.why: Reworded to what two sources support: the months disagree between sources and the greening has one.

claims.claim: Gulf carriers seasonal only; Air India first year-round, Kozhikode then Cochin

claims.why: History with one source. Replaced by the airlines flying now, each with two sources.

claims.claim: terminal newer than its history; four air-conditioned airbridges; lounge opposite the gates
claims.wasBefore: The terminal is newer than the airport's history suggests, with four air conditioned airbridges, a duty free area and an Oman Air lounge opposite the gates for Business and First passengers and for Gold and Silver Sinbad cardholders.
claims.why: The airbridge count is contradicted: the Civil Aviation Authority lists 8 passenger boarding bridges, Wikipedia four. The opening year, the lounge and duty free are kept above.

claims.claim: 1935 RAF airfield, military through the Jebel Akhdar and Dhofar wars, civilian from 1977
claims.wasBefore: It began in 1935 as a Royal Air Force airfield and stayed military through the Jebel Akhdar and Dhofar wars, opening to civilian traffic in 1977.
claims.why: 1935 is unsettled (rafweb has RAF detachments from 1927); the wars have only Wikipedia (the RAF Museum pages refuse both fetchers); and rafweb says the RAF station was already serving civil aircraft from 1951, which contradicts 'opening to civilian traffic in 1977'. Softened to the RAF airfield that closed in 1977.
